idiom_name: PStore#transaction (stdlib) or a Sequel/ActiveRecord model behind a Queue
implementation_notes: Ruby's standard library already contains an atomic durable store: PStore wraps a file in a Hash-like API whose transaction block takes an exclusive lock, reads, yields and writes back atomically, so the copy is store.transaction { |ps| ps[id] = record } with no schema at all - the classic Store object becomes one call. When the store must be shared between processes or live with the application database, the same pattern is a Sequel dataset or ActiveRecord model (one row per record, index on recorded_at and channel) with a retention job deleting by age. In both cases the tap is a background Thread with a Queue, or an ActiveJob, so the sender never waits on the store. Hand-writing a Store class is only justified when the store backend must be swappable; otherwise the model (or PStore) plus the tap is the pattern.
code_sketch:
require "pstore"
store = PStore.new("messages.pstore")
queue = Queue.new
Thread.new do                               # tap: exactly one writer thread
    loop do
        rec = queue.pop
        store.transaction { |ps| ps[rec[:id]] = rec }
    rescue => e
        warn "message store drop: #{e.class}"   # never re-raise into the sender
    end
end
def tap(queue, msg, body) = queue << { id: msg.message_id, chan: msg.channel, body: body }
pitfalls: PStore keeps the whole file in memory and takes an exclusive lock per transaction: it is a single-process store, and two processes (or a fork) writing the same file block or corrupt each other.
ActiveRecord/Sequel writes on the request path inherit the application database's availability; put the tap behind a background job so a slow database degrades the audit trail instead of the API.
Marshal-based PStore files are coupled to your class definitions: refactoring the stored record can make old files unreadable, so store plain hashes or JSON if the shape will evolve.
A rescue inside the loop hides the failure and the record together; count drops and alert, or the store's holes stay invisible.
